To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the third-party doctrine fails to recognize the privacy expectations of individuals who use technology corporations to communicate and share information; corporations are unlikely to serve as effective avatars for the people in the face of government surveillance because corporations have strong incentives to cooperate; corporations have a dubious history of serving as Fourth Amendment avatars; and, finally, the third-party problem is a product of the government’s use of private industry to facilitate surveillance, which has its roots in English law.
The third-party doctrine is a poor proxy for the individual’s right to challenge government surveillance.
